section.title: Solomon's Wedding Procession
section.sectionRationale: A new voice cries out as a splendid procession rises from the wilderness in a column of perfumed smoke: it is King Solomon’s carriage, guarded by sixty mighty men, coming on his wedding day. The scene lifts love from the private world of the lovers into public, royal celebration, crowned by the king in the day of his heart’s rejoicing.
section.thesis: Love arrives in public splendor: the king comes in a guarded, perfumed procession on his wedding day, and the daughters of Zion are called to come out and gaze at the crowned bridegroom in the day of his heart’s rejoicing.
section.frameNote: Two movements: the question and the sight, who is this coming up from the wilderness, revealed as Solomon’s guarded carriage; and the call to behold the crowned king on his wedding day, the day of his heart’s rejoicing.

verses.text: Who is this coming up from the wilderness like a column of smoke, scented with myrrh and frankincense from all the spices of the merchant?
Behold, it is Solomon’s carriage, escorted by sixty of the mightiest men of Israel.
All are skilled with the sword, experienced in warfare. Each has his sword at his side prepared for the terror of the night.
King Solomon has made his carriage out of the timber of Lebanon.
He has made its posts of silver, its base of gold, its seat of purple fabric. Its interior is inlaid with {{ahavah|love}} by the daughters of Jerusalem.

units.label: Behold the crowned king
units.note: the day of his heart's rejoicing

verses.text: Come out, O daughters of Zion, and gaze at King Solomon, wearing the crown with which his mother crowned him on the day of his {{chatunnah|wedding}}, the day of his heart’s rejoicing.

ahavah.gloss: Love. The very interior of the king’s carriage is said to be inlaid or fitted out with love; the whole procession is framed and furnished by love, ahavah, the word that crowns the Song.

chatunnah.gloss: Wedding, the day of espousal. This is the only appearance of this word in the Old Testament, marking the joyful wedding day of the king, called the day of his heart’s rejoicing.

basic.context: A watcher cries out as a grand procession rises from the wilderness in a pillar of fragrant smoke. It is King Solomon’s royal carriage, guarded by sixty of Israel’s best soldiers, built of the finest timber and gold, its inside fitted out with love. The daughters of Zion are called to come and see the king wearing his wedding crown on the happiest day of his life. Love here becomes public, royal, and celebrated.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a wedding poem, a set piece of royal splendor. On the plain level it lifts the lovers’ private joy into a public celebration worthy of a king’s wedding. Within the whole Bible, the picture of a crowned king coming to his wedding, guarded and glorious, points forward to Christ the King and His wedding day. The literal splendor opens onto the gospel.
basic.originalLanguages: The carriage is inlaid with ahavah, love, the word that runs through the Song. And the day is called the king’s chatunnah, his wedding, a word found only here in the Old Testament, matched with the phrase the day of his heart’s rejoicing. The whole scene is love made public and crowned with joy.
basic.typology: A crowned king coming to his wedding, guarded against every terror of the night, pictures Christ the King who comes for His bride. The joy of the wedding day anticipates the marriage supper of the Lamb.
basic.christ: Solomon, crowned and rejoicing on his wedding day, is a shadow of the greater King. Christ is the Bridegroom who comes for His church, crowned now with glory, whose heart rejoices over His people, and whose wedding day the whole story is moving toward. The daughters of Zion are called to come and gaze; so are we.
basic.god: God delights in the joy of a wedding and is not aloof from human celebration. More than that, He is preparing a wedding of His own, the union of Christ and His people, over which His heart rejoices as a bridegroom rejoices over his bride.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 62:5, as a bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so your God will rejoice over you. Revelation 19:7, the marriage of the Lamb has come. Psalm 45, a royal wedding psalm for the king.
basic.oneStory: The wedding procession lifts love into public splendor and joy. It points beyond Solomon to Christ the King, whose wedding day the Bible is moving toward, when the Bridegroom will rejoice over His bride forever.

context.literary:
The poem is one sweeping scene, built as a question and its answer. It opens with 'Who is this', a question the Song asks again at 6:10 and 8:5, and each time the answer turns the reader's eyes somewhere new. Here the answer comes in verse 7 with 'Behold', and the camera moves steadily closer: first a rising column of scented smoke on the horizon, then the carriage, then the sixty guards, then the timber, silver, gold and purple of the couch, and finally the king's own head and the crown on it. The scene begins with distance and mystery and ends with a close and personal command, 'gaze', where it began with a question.

The grammar of verse 6 holds a puzzle. The Hebrew word for 'this' is feminine, so the opening question seems to ask about a woman, or about the feminine noun for the carriage, yet verse 7 names the carriage as Solomon's and the poem finishes on the king. Some hear the bride arriving in her bridegroom's carriage; others hear the whole cortege as one fragrant cloud. The ambiguity is probably intended, since bride, carriage and king arrive together as a single event.

The unit also sits at a pointed place in the book. The scene before it, 3:1-5, is a private night of longing that ends with the bride holding her beloved and charging the daughters of Jerusalem not to rouse love before its time. This scene answers that night with a public day of rejoicing, and the audience changes from the daughters of Jerusalem to the daughters of Zion, who are no longer warned but invited. The poet also loads the verses with a cluster of detail about security, wealth and craft before the single word of feeling arrives in verse 10, so that love appears as the thing the whole splendid vehicle was built to hold.
context.historical:
Solomon's reign, which the book's title in 1:1 connects with the Song, was a time of building and trade. He had cedar of Lebanon cut and floated down the coast through his arrangement with Hiram of Tyre, 1 Kings 5:6-10, and his throne was made of ivory overlaid with pure gold, 1 Kings 10:18. In the same chapter silver is said to have been as common in Jerusalem as stones, 1 Kings 10:27. The carriage with its silver posts and golden base is in keeping with what the historical books say of his court, and the first hearers would have heard it as the language of royal splendor rather than as an exaggeration.

The fragrance of verse 6 points to the incense routes. Myrrh and frankincense came from the south of Arabia, and the spices of a travelling merchant were among the costliest goods of the day; the queen of Sheba herself brought spices to Solomon in large quantity, 1 Kings 10:10. A procession scented like that, rising on the road from the wilderness, announces wealth before it announces a person.

The sixty guards, 'skilled with the sword', fit a world where roads were dangerous, and where wedding processions moved in the evening by lamplight, as the parable of Matthew 25:1-6 assumes. Sixty is a large royal escort, in the same register as the mighty men who surrounded David. The 'terror of the night' is a real fear, as Psalm 91:5 shows, and not a figure of speech.

Wedding customs in Israel included a procession in which the bride was brought to the bridegroom's house in joyful company, Psalm 45:13-15, and the bridegroom wore a headdress or crown, Isaiah 61:10. The mother's crowning in verse 11 has no parallel narrative in the historical books. It may reflect a custom, or it may be a poetic way of saying that his mother's blessing was on the match. Solomon's own marriage to Pharaoh's daughter is recorded in 1 Kings 3:1, and a royal wedding of that kind would indeed have been a public event.
context.canonical:
Within the Song itself, this poem is the first of three 'who is this' questions, and it is paired most closely with 8:5, where the same words are asked of the woman who comes up from the wilderness leaning on her beloved. The Song thus closes the circle it opened here: the splendid arrival of the king in chapter 3 is matched by the humble leaning of the bride at the end.

Elsewhere in Scripture a royal wedding is a recurring picture. Psalm 45 is a wedding song for a king, with its glorious princess led to him in colorful garments. Isaiah 62:5 promises that God will rejoice over His people as a bridegroom over his bride, and Isaiah 61:10 clothes the redeemed like a bridegroom with a headdress and a bride with jewels. Jesus takes up the same picture when He calls Himself the bridegroom whose guests cannot mourn while He is with them, Matthew 9:15, and tells of a king who gave a wedding banquet for his son, Matthew 22:2. John the Baptist is the bridegroom's friend who listens for his voice and is full of joy, John 3:29.

The New Testament ends on the day this poem anticipates. 'The marriage of the Lamb has come, and His bride has made herself ready,' Revelation 19:7, and the holy city descends 'prepared as a bride adorned for her husband,' Revelation 21:2. Solomon himself becomes a measuring stick: Jesus says that 'One greater than Solomon is here,' Matthew 12:42, and the Song's crowned bridegroom stands among the shadows that this greater king fills.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The poet wants the reader to see that marriage is worth celebrating in public and worth guarding. The long list of precautions, sixty swordsmen and the dread of the night, tells the first hearers that love is precious enough to be defended, and the carriage with its costly materials tells them that it is honored. Nothing in the poem is cheap or hidden.

The scene also teaches by where it stands. It follows a night when the bride sought her beloved alone and found him at last, and it follows the charge not to arouse love before its time. The wedding procession is the proper end of that waiting: love that was kept for its time arrives openly, with the community called to watch. The poet means the hearers to feel that desire given room to wait is not lessened but crowned.

The reference to the crown his mother set on him adds a further note. A marriage is not only the business of two people. Family blessing, community witness and royal dignity all gather around the day, and the poem wants the hearer to rejoice with the groom rather than merely observe him.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage describes a royal wedding and gives no instruction. Nothing in it tells a couple to spend lavishly, to travel with guards or to build a carriage of silver and gold. The Torah in fact warns the king against multiplying wives and piling up silver and gold, Deuteronomy 17:17, and 1 Kings 11:1-3 records how Solomon's many wives turned his heart. The poem therefore cannot be read as an endorsement of everything about Solomon's household.

What carries over is the principle beneath the splendor. A wedding deserves public honor, a marriage deserves protection, and joy is a fitting response to the beginning of a covenant. A modest wedding in a village church and a royal procession in ancient Jerusalem share the same truth: two people publicly pledged to each other are a gift to be celebrated.

For the believer, the descriptive splendor also functions as a pointer. The Bible takes up wedding language for Christ and His church, so the passage is best used to cultivate gladness about the Lord's coming, and not as a pattern for budgets.

debates.question: What kind of book is the Song: a celebration of married love, an allegory of Christ and the church, or both?

views.label: A celebration of covenant married love
views.case: The scene is a royal wedding procession, the public celebration of a marriage; it fits most naturally the joy of a real wedding, which Scripture honors, Psalm 45 and Genesis 2.

views.label: An allegory of Christ and the church, or God and Israel
views.case: The church has long seen in the crowned king coming to his wedding a picture of Christ the King and His bride, in step with the Bible’s bridegroom imagery, Isaiah 62 and Revelation 19.

views.label: Both, the literal wedding as a God-given sign
views.case: The fullest reading keeps both: the poem truly celebrates a royal wedding, and because marriage is a God-given sign of Christ and the church, Ephesians 5:31 to 32, the crowned bridegroom rightly points to the greater King and His wedding day.

debates.bearing: Holding both keeps the wedding joy earthy and real while letting it point to the marriage of the Lamb, so the passage neither becomes bare pageantry nor loses its gospel horizon.

debates.question: Who is coming up from the wilderness in verse 6?

views.label: Solomon, in his carriage
views.case: Verse 7 identifies the carriage as Solomon's and verse 11 ends on the king, so the procession is his arrival to claim his bride. The feminine 'this' can be explained by the feminine noun for the couch, or by the feminine form of the question, which agrees with the cortege as a whole.

views.label: The bride, carried in the carriage
views.case: The question uses the feminine 'this', and the same words are asked of the bride in 8:5. On this reading the carriage carries the bride to the wedding, and the king awaits her. Psalm 45:13-15 pictures a bride led to the king in procession.

views.label: The whole wedding cortege
views.case: The poem does not try to separate bride, carriage and king. The column of perfumed smoke is the entire company, and the question is answered by describing everything that makes it up, which is why the scene moves from smoke to guards to the crown.

debates.bearing: The poem's silence about who sits inside suggests that the answer is less important than the effect. Whether the focus falls on the king or on the bride, the whole picture is of love honored and defended, and either reading leads to the same call to rejoice.

debates.question: Is Solomon the hero of the Song or a foil to the true beloved?

views.label: Solomon is the bridegroom throughout
views.case: The title in 1:1 connects the book to Solomon, and 1:4 and 1:12 speak of the king in the first person without a hint of contrast. In this reading the royal wedding of chapter 3 is simply his.

views.label: Solomon is a rival or foil
views.case: Some interpreters have read the Song as a drama in which a shepherd is the true lover and Solomon a wealthy rival who tries to win the woman. 8:11-12 plays with Solomon's vineyard, and 1 Kings 11 shows how far his love of many women was from the Song's single-hearted ideal.

views.label: Solomon as the poet's ideal image, with his flaws left outside the frame
views.case: The poet borrows Solomon as the model of royal love without claiming that his real household was ideal. The Song uses him as a type of the king whose wedding is glorious, while the historical books record his failure.

debates.bearing: Most careful readers take Solomon as the bridegroom, but the foil reading is a reminder that the historical Solomon did not live up to the Song's pattern. That tension is part of what makes the passage point beyond Solomon to a greater king.

study.originalLanguages:
The opening phrase, 'Who is this', uses the feminine form of the demonstrative, which is why the identity of the traveller is debated. The verb for 'coming up' is the usual one for travelling toward Jerusalem, which sits on high ground, so the poem pictures a pilgrim-like approach to the city.

The scented cloud is described by a participle from the root that means to make smoke, the same root used of burnt incense in the sanctuary, Exodus 30:7-8. The reader may therefore hear the language of worship in the air of a wedding. Myrrh and frankincense are the two spices named, and the 'spices of the merchant' are literally the powders of a trader, a reminder that all this fragrance was bought and carried from far away.

The carriage in verse 7 is a word usually meaning a bed or couch, as when King David bows in worship on his bed, 1 Kings 1:47. The BSB footnote explains it as the couch on which servants carry a king, which is why it is translated 'carriage'. In verse 9 a different word is used, a rare one whose meaning is drawn from its context, and it too is translated as a carriage or litter. The poet thus uses two words for the same thing, a variation that sets the object in a slightly different light each time.

The guards are 'mighty men', the word used elsewhere of David's elite warriors. They are described as 'skilled with the sword', which in Hebrew pictures men gripping the sword, and as 'experienced in warfare', literally taught in war. The night they fear is 'the terror of the night', where the Hebrew word for terror is the ordinary word for dread, the same pairing found in Psalm 91:5.

The couch is 'inlaid with love', and the Hebrew allows more than one reading of the closing words 'by the daughters of Jerusalem'. Either love is the material that fills the inlay, or the daughters themselves fitted it out lovingly, or the interior was paved with an expression of love from them. The difference in English is small, but each version gives the daughters of Jerusalem a stake in the king's wedding.

Finally, the crown in verse 11 is a word for a wreath or crown given for honor, and the wedding day is also 'the day of his heart's rejoicing', where the word for rejoicing is the usual word for gladness. Jeremiah 33:11 pairs gladness and joy with the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride, so the vocabulary of this verse is the vocabulary of wedding celebration across the Old Testament.

typology.fulfillment: Solomon is borne in a carriage of cedar, silver, gold and purple, surrounded by swordsmen. Christ also comes to His city as King, but He rides a donkey, 'righteous and victorious, humble,' Zechariah 9:9, in answer to the cry of the daughters of Zion, and He tells Pilate that His servants will not fight, John 18:36. The type is escalated and inverted: the true king's glory is not in the guard around him but in the humility with which He comes to win His bride. It falls short because Solomon's silver and gold could not secure a faithful heart, 1 Kings 11:3.

typology.type: The crown on the wedding day, 3:11
typology.fulfillment: The king wears the crown his mother set on him, and the daughters of Zion are bidden to gaze. Jesus, too, is crowned and shown to the crowd: soldiers twist a crown of thorns and dress Him in purple, and Pilate says 'Here is your King,' John 19:2, 5, 14. The correspondence is deliberately painful, since the crown that mocks Him is the one that carries Him to the cross and to the glory of Hebrews 2:9, where He is 'now crowned with glory and honor because He suffered death.' The type falls short because Solomon's crown was a sign of wealth and ease; Christ's crown is won by suffering.

typology.type: The escort against the terror of the night, 3:7-8
typology.fulfillment: The sixty armed men guard the procession against every dread of the dark. The Lord Himself is the Protector of Israel who 'will neither slumber nor sleep,' Psalm 121:4, and Jesus keeps those the Father gave Him, John 10:28. Jude 24 speaks of Him who is able to keep believers from stumbling and present them in His glory. The type falls short because swords and men can fail; Christ's keeping cannot.

typology.type: The day of his heart's rejoicing, 3:11
typology.fulfillment: The wedding day is called a day of joy for the bridegroom's heart. That joy is the pattern for the day toward which Scripture moves: Isaiah 62:5 says that as a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so God will rejoice over His people, and Revelation 19:7 announces that the marriage of the Lamb has come. Zephaniah 3:17 adds that the Lord will rejoice over His people with singing. The type falls short because Solomon's rejoicing was one groom's among many wives; Christ's is for one bride, the church, and it will not end.

study.christ:
The poem leads to Christ first by the figure of the king. Solomon is the son of David whom God promised to establish, 2 Samuel 7:12-13, and the Gospels delight in calling Jesus the Son of David. Yet Jesus Himself measures Solomon and finds him lacking, 'One greater than Solomon is here,' Matthew 12:42. The splendid Solomon of the poem is therefore a shadow of the king whose glory is real, and the poem cannot be read as pointing to Solomon alone.

It leads to Him also by the figure of the bridegroom. Jesus calls Himself the bridegroom whose guests cannot fast while He is with them, Matthew 9:15, and Paul says he promised the church to one husband to present her as a pure virgin to Christ, 2 Corinthians 11:2. The wedding day of Song 3:11 is the day toward which the whole New Testament moves, the marriage of the Lamb in Revelation 19:7.

The invitation to the daughters of Zion to 'come out and gaze' has a strange echo in the Gospel of John. After the soldiers set the crown of thorns on His head and clothe Him in purple, Pilate presents Him with the words 'Here is the man' and 'Here is your King,' John 19:5, 14. The crowned king displayed for the watching crowd is real, but the scene is a mockery of royalty, and it hides the true coronation. The Song's crown is the crown of a happy day; Christ's crown of thorns is the crown of the day He wins His bride, and Hebrews 2:9 says that He is now crowned with glory and honor because He suffered death.

The poem also leads to Christ by contrast. Solomon's carriage is guarded by sixty men because he needs guarding. Jesus rejects the sword, John 18:36, and goes to His wedding by way of the cross, protecting His people by laying down His own life.

It is wise not to allegorize each item, so that the cedar or the silver is made to stand for some doctrine. The posts, base and seat are not given separate meanings in the text. The point is the whole picture of a crowned king coming for his bride with every precaution and every joy, which the New Testament itself uses for Christ.
study.god:
The passage shows a God who is not suspicious of splendor and celebration. The Bible as a whole condemns pride and covetousness, but it does not treat a wedding feast as a worldly distraction. The Lord Himself provides the picture of a king's wedding for His own purposes, and Jesus attends a wedding at Cana, John 2:1-2, and chooses a wedding feast to describe the kingdom, Matthew 22:2. The God of this poem is the one who has made human joy and is glad when it is publicly shared.

The scene also shows God as the keeper of what He loves. The sixty guards are the poem's way of saying that precious things must be protected, and Scripture says the same of God: the Protector of Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps, Psalm 121:4, and the believer does not need to fear the terror of the night, Psalm 91:5. Power and tenderness are joined. The vehicle that is armed for war is inlaid with love, which is a fair picture of a God who is mighty to save and who also rejoices over His people with singing, Zephaniah 3:17.

There is a tension the passage invites us to hold. The Song portrays a royal wedding, yet the historical Solomon failed in his own marriages, 1 Kings 11:1-3, and the Torah expressly warned the king against taking many wives, Deuteronomy 17:17. God lets a flawed king stand as a figure of a faithful one, and by contrast with the failure shows what faithful love would look like. That is a form of His patience and also of His promise, since He does not discard the picture because the human instrument fell short.

For worship, the passage gives language for rejoicing. The people of God are invited to come out and look at their King and to be glad on His wedding day. That means praise is not only quiet reverence but also a public delight in the One who comes for His people, with gladness equal to the joy He takes in them, Isaiah 62:5.

crossReferences.note: The source of the carriage's cedar. Solomon's agreement with Hiram of Tyre to cut and float Lebanon's timber to Jerusalem shows where the poem's materials came from. The Song's 'timber of Lebanon' in 3:9 is a deliberate reminder of the same royal building program that raised the temple.

Solomon's throne of ivory overlaid with pure gold. It confirms that the carriage's silver and gold are not poetic exaggeration but match what the historical books say about the king's court, and shows the poem borrowing the language of real royal craftsmanship.

The sobering counterpart. The king whose wedding the Song praises had seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines, and they turned his heart. The contrast shows why the Song's ideal of single love finds its true fulfilment beyond Solomon.

A royal wedding psalm in which the princess is led to the king in colorful garments, with her companions, in joy and gladness. It is the closest parallel to the procession of Song 3:6-11 and shows that a wedding procession for a king was a recognized subject of Israel's praise.

The phrase 'terror of the night' in Song 3:8 appears here as something the one who trusts God need not fear. Where the Song relies on swordsmen, the psalm points to God Himself as the guard, and so deepens what the sixty men are protecting against.

A prophetic promise that lifts the groom's gladness from Song 3:11 into God's own heart. The Lord is pictured as the one whose delight in His redeemed people matches a young husband's delight on his wedding day.

John the Baptist describes himself as the bridegroom's friend who stands and listens and is overjoyed at the bridegroom's voice. It echoes the Song's wedding company and identifies Jesus as the bridegroom they have been waiting for.

Jesus says that One greater than Solomon is here. The words invite the reader to measure the Song's king against Christ and to see that the splendid carriage and crown of Solomon are shadows of a King who is greater.

The daughter of Zion is told that her King comes to her, righteous, victorious and humble on a donkey. Set beside Song 3:11, where the daughters of Zion are called to gaze at their king, it shows a different kind of royal arrival and fulfils the call in Christ.

The marriage of the Lamb has come and His bride has made herself ready, clothed in bright, pure linen. This is the day to which the Song's wedding day points, with Christ as the bridegroom and the church as the bride.

The same question, 'Who is this coming up from the wilderness,' is asked again at the end of the book, but now the answer is a woman leaning on her beloved. The Song's final scene softens the pomp of chapter 3 into the closeness it was meant to serve.

study.oneStory:
This procession belongs to the larger story of a God who makes a people for Himself and brings them to a wedding. In creation, the first marriage was celebrated before any sin entered the world, when the man and his wife were naked and not ashamed, Genesis 2:25. The Song takes that original joy and sets it in a royal and public frame, so that the reader is reminded that marriage was a gift of creation before it was ever a custom of any nation.

The fall did not remove marriage, but it strained it, and the Old Testament is full of marriages that fail, including the household of the very king whose wedding the poem sings, 1 Kings 11:3. That is why the Song cannot be the last word. Its picture of a crowned king, a faithful bride and a day of rejoicing is true to what marriage was meant to be, and yet no earthly wedding fully keeps the promise. The prophets therefore turn the language of the wedding toward God's own purpose. Isaiah promises that as a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so the Lord will rejoice over His people, Isaiah 62:5, and Hosea hears the Lord promise to betroth His people to Himself forever, Hosea 2:19-20.

Redemption arrives in Christ, the greater Solomon, who comes humble to Jerusalem, is crowned with thorns, and gives Himself for the church, Ephesians 5:25-27. He is the bridegroom whose guests cannot mourn while He is with them, Matthew 9:15, and who tells of a king making a wedding feast for his son, Matthew 22:2.

The story ends with a wedding. John hears a great multitude proclaim that the marriage of the Lamb has come, Revelation 19:7, and sees the holy city coming down from God like a bride adorned for her husband, Revelation 21:2. The procession from the wilderness reaches its end here, where the bride is no longer carried through a dangerous night but brought home to a city with no night in it. The Song's carriage and crown are the early sketch of that day, and the daughters of Zion who were told to come and gaze become the whole redeemed people.

quiz.q: What is coming up from the wilderness in 3:6 to 7?

options.text: King Solomon’s wedding procession, a perfumed, guarded royal carriage.
options.note: The pillar of fragrant smoke reveals the king’s glorious wedding procession.

options.text: An invading army bent on destruction.
options.note: Armed guards do surround it, but the scene is a wedding procession, not an army bent on destruction.
The procession is indeed perfumed with the merchant’s fragrant powders, but it is King Solomon’s wedding carriage, not a caravan of ordinary merchants.
It is a wedding, the day of the king’s heart’s rejoicing, not a funeral.

quiz.q: Why are the sixty mighty men present in 3:7 to 8?

options.text: To guard the king’s procession, swords ready against the terror of the night.
options.note: They are an armed escort protecting the wedding journey.
They are indeed armed warriors expert in war, but they guard the king’s procession against the terror of the night; they do not attack the bride’s family.
They are warriors escorting the king, not traders.

options.text: To compete for the bride themselves.
options.note: They do surround the bridal carriage, but as protectors of the king, not as rivals competing for the bride.

quiz.q: What are the daughters of Zion called to do in 3:11?

options.text: Come out and gaze at King Solomon, crowned on the day of his wedding and heart’s rejoicing.
options.note: The climax is a call to behold the crowned, rejoicing bridegroom.

options.text: Stay hidden and take no notice of the king.
options.note: They are summoned to come out and gaze at him.
They are indeed summoned to respond to the king, but with rejoicing on his wedding day, not mourning a departure.
The crown is truly in view, but it is his mother who crowned him; the daughters are called to come out and behold him crowned, not to crown him.

quiz.q: How does the crowned bridegroom point to Christ?

options.text: He foreshadows Christ the King and Bridegroom, crowned with glory, coming for His bride, whose wedding day the whole story awaits.
options.note: The scene points to the marriage supper of the Lamb.

options.text: He teaches that only kings can be loved.
options.note: The scene does exalt a king, but the point is the royal wedding as a sign of Christ, not that only kings can be loved.

options.text: He shows that God takes no delight in weddings.
options.note: The opposite: God rejoices as a bridegroom over his bride, Isaiah 62.

options.text: He has no connection to Christ at all.
options.note: The scene truly depicts a real royal wedding, yet Scripture reads the crowned bridegroom as a picture of Christ and His church, so it does point beyond itself.

questions: The wedding lifts private love into public, joyful celebration. Where might God be inviting you to rejoice openly in His goodness rather than keeping your joy hidden?
The king’s carriage is guarded against the terror of the night. How does it comfort you that Christ guards His people through every darkness on the way to the wedding?
The daughters of Zion are called to come out and gaze at the crowned king. What would it look like this week to fix your gaze on Christ the King and rejoice?
It is called the day of the king’s heart’s rejoicing. Have you considered that Christ’s joy is to have you as His own, and how might that reshape how you see yourself?
The whole story moves toward the marriage supper of the Lamb. How does living in hope of that wedding day change the way you face this week?

translationNotes.note: Who is this coming up from the wilderness opens the wedding scene and is echoed of the bride in 8:5.
Solomon’s carriage renders a word for a portable couch or litter on which servants carried the king.
Wedding here translates a Hebrew word found only in this verse; the day of his heart’s rejoicing marks it as a day of great gladness.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched from bible.helloao.org for Song of Solomon 3:6-11, chapter 3. Poetic lines rendered as flowing prose within each verse.
